catalog_quote: Lha’alua distinguishes primary stress (indicated by ˊ) and secondary stress (indicated by ˋ). Primary stress is not contrastive, nor is secondary stress. [...] The primary stress within a word in Lha’alua typically falls either on the penultimate or antepenultimate syllable. When a word has two syllables, which is less common in Lha’alua, the penultimate syllable bears primary stress. When a word has three or more syllables, primary stress falls on the penultimate or antepenultimate syllable. For some Lha’alua words, the syllable with primary stress may vary freely from speaker to speaker and even within the usage of the same speaker. [...] (2.16) a. /sa.rí.a/ or /sá.ri.a/ ‘house/home’ b. /ta.ɫá.kɨ/ or /tá.ɫa.kɨ/ ‘pig’ c. /va.ná.u/ or /vá.na.u/ ‘female name’ d. /sa.sú.a/ or /sá.su.a/ ‘two (people)’ There is one primary stress per word. [...] Note that the primary stress within a word in Lha’alua falls either on the penultimate or antepenultimate syllable, even if there is any stress shift. [...] When long vowels appear, they usually bear primary stress or secondary stress, as in (2.20). They bear the primary stress, when there are more than two syllables (including two syllables) in a word, and it falls on the penultimate or antepenultimate syllable. They carry the secondary stress while a word has more than three syllables. (2.20) a. /ɫúː.ɫu.ŋu/ ‘river’ b. /mɨ́ː.mɨ.a/ ‘also’ c. /máː.taː.ta/ ‘tomorrow’ d. /kíːra/ ‘yesterday’ e. /pùː.si.á.mɨ/ ‘rice plant’

new_statements.citation: Pan, Chia-jung. 2012. A Grammar of Lha'alua, an Austronesian Language of Taiwan. PhD thesis, James Cook University. xxiv+389 pp.https://researchonline.jcu.edu.au/32386/
new_statements.locator: §2.3.1 'Primary and secondary stress assignment', pp. 35-36 (pp. 65-66); §2.3.2 'Stress shift', pp. 36-38
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (419 pp., LibreOffice text, not encrypted). §2.3 Stress begins on printed p. 35 = p. 65; §2.3.1 'Primary and secondary stress assignment' pp. 35-36, §2.3.2 'Stress shift' pp. 36-38, exactly as the locator says. The quoted passage is there verbatim: 'Lha'alua distinguishes primary stress (indicated by ˊ) and secondary stress (indicated by ˋ). Primary stress is not contrastive, nor is secondary stress.' then (after two skipped sentences on pitch/intensity and the denial of pitch accent status, correctly marked '[..]') 'The primary stress within a word in Lha'alua typically falls either on the penultimate or antepenultimate syllable. When a word has two syllables, which is less common i…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Non-contrastive primary stress confined to a two-syllable right-edge window: penultimate in disyllables; penultimate OR antepenultimate in longer words, with free variation between the two positions across and within speakers for some words (author's examples 2.16 give the same word with either placement). The window is computed over the phonological word including suffixes and enclitics (stress shifts rightward when these attach, staying penult/antepenult). Long vowels usually attract primary stress. Closest fixed-list codes would be fixed: penultimate syllable/fixed: antepenultimate syllable, but the source explicitly refuses to fix one of them; Li & Chen 2023 p. 3 independently state the same: 'Stress falls on the penultimate or antepenultimate syllable. It is not phonemic.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress only in monomorphemic/complex words of more than four syllables (author's wording: 'more than four'; examples show 4- and 7-syllable words); only prefixes, never suffixes or enclitics, can carry it; it shifts leftward onto newly added prefixes, and leftward shift is applied before rightward shift. Words with fewer than four syllables have none.
new_statements.exceptions: Free inter-/intra-speaker variation between penult and antepenult in some words (e.g. /sa.Ri.a/ 'house', /ta.ɬa.ki/ 'pig'); primary stress shifts with suffixes/enclitics but not with voice markers; stressed long vowels may be shortened in rapid speech after a stress-shifting affix attaches; vowel dropping does not move stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (root/stem plus clitics); statements drawn from elicited words and connected speech, with slow vs. rapid speech noted. Realised with higher pitch and greater intensity; the author explicitly denies that Lha'alua is a pitch accent language.
new_statements.identity_note: Pan 2012 uses the autonym Lha'alua (ɫaʔalua) for the language known as Saaroa (Asai's 1931 mistranscription, per Li & Chen 2023 p. 1 n. 1); same language, ISO sxr, glottocode saar1237. Spoken in Taoyuan District, Kaohsiung, Taiwan. No dialect split is invoked in the stress section.

new_statements.quote: 在拉阿魯哇語中，重音落在詞的倒數第二或倒數第三音節，例如：maíni「小的」、hláhlusa「男人」、’ʉ’ʉráisa「謝謝」。重音在拉阿魯哇語並沒有辨義作用，在本書中將不標。 [p. 14] ... 拉阿魯哇語詞彙之重音通常落在倒數第二或第三元音上，故名詞sala’a「路」之重音落在倒數第三元音sa上，即sála’a；而當動詞性前綴u-「腳部動作」加綴上在名詞sala’a「路」上形成m-u-sala「去、走路」時，重音則由元音a轉移至元音u上，即músala，重音一樣是保持在倒數第三音節。依附詞通常不影響重音，例如músala加上=aku「我.主格」重音還是一樣músalaaku。 [pp. 22-23]
new_statements.translation: In Lha'alua, stress falls on the penultimate or antepenultimate syllable of the word, e.g. maíni 'small', hláhlusa 'man', 'ʉ'ʉráisa 'thank you'. Stress in Lha'alua has no meaning-distinguishing function, and will not be marked in this book. [p. 14] ... The stress of Lha'alua words usually falls on the penultimate or antepenultimate vowel; thus the stress of the noun sala'a 'road' falls on the antepenultimate vowel sa, i.e. sála'a; and when the verbal prefix u- 'foot action' is attached to the noun sala'a 'road' to form m-u-sala 'go, walk', the stress moves from the vowel a to the vowel u, i.e. músala, the stress still staying on the antepenultimate syllable. Clitics usually do not affect stress; e.g. when músala takes =aku '1SG.NOM' the stress stays the same, músalaaku. [pp. 22-23]

Block PAGE 36 carries printed page number 14 and the heading '2.3.2 重音'; lines 1238-1240 read exactly '在拉阿魯哇語中，重音落在詞的倒數第二或倒數第三音節，例如：maíni「小的」、hláhlusa「男人」、’ʉ’ʉráisa「謝謝」。重音在拉阿魯哇語並沒有辨義作用，在本書中將不標。' Block PAGE 44 (printed 22) ends with '拉阿魯哇語詞彙之重音通常落在倒數第二或第三元音上，故名詞sala’a' and PAGE 45 (printed 23) continues '「路」之重音落在倒數第三元音sa上，即sála’a；…重音則由元音a轉移至元音u上，即músala，重音一樣是保持在倒數第三音節。依附詞通常不影響重音，例如músala加上=aku「我.主格」重音還是一樣músalaaku。' — matches the claimed quote word for word (the compiler ' vs the file's ’ is only an apostrophe glyph). Both page scan show the same text with the acute marks on maíni, hláhlusa, ’ʉ’ʉráisa, sála’a, músala, músalaaku,…
new_statements.relation_note: Same statement as the existing Pan 2012 entry: non-contrastive stress on the penultimate or antepenultimate syllable. It is a condensed version of Pan 2012 §2.3 (no secondary stress, no free variation, no long-vowel attraction), and its example of prefix-driven shift (sála'a -> músala) matches Pan 2012 §2.3.2 'Stress shift'. Minor difference: Pan 2018 says clitics usually do not affect stress (músalaaku), whereas Pan 2012 says the clitics /u/ and /i/ attract stress shift; the placement window is the same in both.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and falls within a two-syllable window at the right edge, on the penultimate or the antepenultimate syllable; the book gives no rule for choosing between the two (examples show both: ma.í.ni penult, hlá.hlu.sa and sá.la.'a antepenult). Affixation re-places the stress so that it stays inside the window (sála'a -> músala); enclitics such as =aku lie outside the stress domain (músalaaku). The book itself does not mark stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; Pan 2018 speaks only of 重音 (stress) without a primary/secondary distinction.
new_statements.exceptions: Prefixation shifts stress to keep it on the antepenult (sála'a -> músala); enclitics usually leave stress unchanged (músalaaku). No lexical exceptions listed; stress is unmarked in the orthography.
new_statements.identity_note: Pan 2018 is the Council of Indigenous Peoples' pedagogical grammar sketch (臺灣南島語言叢書 15) of Lha'alua as spoken in Gaozhong and Taoyuan villages of Taoyuan District and Maya village of Namasia District, Kaohsiung (p. 599 of the text dump, chapter 1); no dialect split is invoked in the stress section. Same author and same variety as the Pan 2012 JCU thesis already in the catalog.

sources.note: §2.3 Stress (pp. 35-38, pp. 65-68): primary and secondary stress, neither contrastive; primary stress on penultimate or antepenultimate syllable (penult in disyllables), with free inter- and intra-speaker variation between the two in some words; secondary stress only in words of 4+ syllables and only on prefixes; suffixes/enclitics shift primary stress rightward but it stays penult/antepenult; long vowels usually bear stress; not a pitch accent language.
